desc:
The grid heights gives the height of the ground in every unit cell of a rectangular field. After a long rain, water collects in the low parts. Water can flow from a cell to its four side neighbours (up, down, left, right) whenever the neighbour's water surface is not higher, and everything that reaches the outside of the grid is lost.

Return the total volume of water that stays trapped, counting one unit of volume for each unit of water depth over each cell.

heights = [[5,5,5],
           [5,1,5],
           [5,5,5]]
-> 4   (the middle cell holds water up to height 5)
heights = [[3,3,3,3],
           [3,1,1,3],
           [3,3,3,3]]
-> 4   (two cells, each filled from 1 to 3)
constraints: All rows have the same length
hints: In one dimension you can use the tallest wall on each side. In two dimensions water can escape through any direction, so the lowest point of the whole boundary matters most.
The water level of a cell is limited by the lowest 'gate' on the best escape path out of the grid. Start from the border cells, which hold no water, and work inwards.

Put all border cells in a min-heap by height. Pop the lowest cell; for each unvisited neighbour, its water level is max(neighbour height, popped level), so it traps max(0, level - height) water. Push the neighbour with that level.
editorial: A cell's final water level is the smallest possible value of 'the highest cell you must cross' over all paths from that cell to the border. Dijkstra-style processing gives this directly: always expand the lowest known boundary of the already-processed region.

Mark all border cells visited and push (height, r, c) into a min-heap. Pop the lowest (level, r, c). For each unvisited neighbour (nr, nc), mark it visited, add max(0, level - heights[nr][nc]) to the answer, and push it with level max(level, heights[nr][nc]). The popped level is the lowest wall of the current frontier, so any neighbour lower than it is guaranteed to fill up to exactly that level - water cannot leak because every other part of the frontier is at least as high.
Each cell is pushed and popped once, so the time is O(R C log(R C)) and the space is O(R C). Grids with fewer than three rows or columns have no interior and trap nothing.
